hook: Your model never sees letters, only integers. How you cut text into them sets cost, context length and what it can learn.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GPT never sees a single letter. It sees integers. How you cut text into integers decides how much every token costs.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-2 has a 50,257-token vocabulary, Llama 3 has 128,256, GPT-4o's o200k has about 200k. Attention cost grows with sequence length squared, so the tokenizer quietly sets your compute bill and your effective context window. This module builds the GPT-2 tokenizer, following CS336 Assignment 1.

1:00 INTUITION — Three ways to cut. Words: short sequences, but a vocabulary that never ends and no answer for typos. Characters: Unicode has about 150,000 assigned code points, and sequences get long. Bytes: only 256 symbols, never out of vocabulary, but sequences get even longer. Subword tokenization is the compromise. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — UTF-8 encodes a code point in 1 to 4 bytes: ASCII is 1 byte, most accented Latin 2, Hindi and Telugu 3, emoji 4. Compression ratio = bytes / tokens. Attention FLOPs per layer scale as T^2 d, so halving T cuts attention cost by 4x and the MLP cost by 2x. Embedding plus output head parameters scale as 2 V d untied, V d tied.

5:00 CODE — text = a paragraph of English, a line of Python, a Telugu sentence, and an emoji line. ords = [ord(c) for c in text]; bs = list(text.encode('utf-8')); words = text.split(). Print len of each and the vocab each would need. Show 'hello'.encode('utf-8') vs '\u0c24\u0c46\u0c32\u0c41\u0c17\u0c41'.encode('utf-8') (the word Telugu in Telugu script) and count bytes per character. Then tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2').encode(text) for the subword count.

8:30 RECEIPT — assert bytes(bs).decode('utf-8') == text (bytes round-trip losslessly). assert all(0 <= b < 256 for b in bs). For the English paragraph, bytes / gpt2 tokens comes out near 4, matching the commonly quoted roughly 4 characters per token for English. For the Telugu sentence, the ratio collapses toward 1 or below, measured live.
10:00 MEASURE — Table with rows English, code, Telugu, emoji and columns chars, bytes, words, GPT-2 tokens, bytes per token. The Telugu row is the punchline: same meaning, several times more tokens.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — Bytes give you a closed 256-symbol alphabet; subwords give you compression on top. Interview line: tokenization sets sequence length, and sequence length sets attention cost, so a bad tokenizer for a language is a tax on every user of that language.
11:30 NEXT — Next: Byte Pair Encoding by hand.
key_math: UTF-8: 1-4 bytes per code point;  compression = bytes/tokens;  attention FLOPs per layer ~ 4 T^2 d (forward);  embedding params = V d
code_task: why_tok.py: compare(text) -> dict(chars=len(text), bytes=len(text.encode('utf-8')), words=len(text.split()), gpt2=len(tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2').encode(text))) for four sample texts; print a table.
receipt: assert bytes(list(text.encode('utf-8'))).decode('utf-8') == text for all samples; assert max(text.encode('utf-8')) < 256; English bytes/token approximately 4 with the gpt2 encoding.
gotchas: Confusing len(text) (code points) with len(text.encode()) (bytes); slicing a bytes object mid-character and getting UnicodeDecodeError on decode; assuming one emoji is one character, many are several code points joined by zero-width joiners
interview_q: Why do modern LLMs use byte-level tokenizers instead of character-level ones? Answer: bytes give a fixed 256-symbol base vocabulary that can represent any string with no unknown tokens, and BPE merges on top recover the compression that raw bytes lack.
explainer: To a language model, text is not letters. It is a list of integers. The question is where to cut.
Cut at words and sequences are short, but the vocabulary never ends. Every typo is a brand new word.
Cut at characters and Unicode alone has around a hundred fifty thousand of them. Sequences get long too.
Cut at bytes and there are only two hundred fifty six symbols. Nothing is ever out of vocabulary.
But UTF-8 spends one byte on an English letter, three on a Telugu letter, four on an emoji.
Subword tokens are the compromise. Common chunks become one token, rare things fall back to bytes.
Same sentence, different languages. English costs a few tokens. The Telugu translation costs several times more.

Two token-count bars, short for English, much longer for Telugu, with a multiplier label.

x_post: UTF-8 spends 1 byte on 'a', 3 on a Telugu letter, 4 on an emoji. Byte-level BPE builds on that 256-symbol base. Measured: English is ~4 bytes/token in GPT-2; Telugu is close to 1. Same meaning, several times the cost. Code + video: [link]

English compresses to about 4 bytes per GPT-2 token; Telugu barely compresses at all, which means more tokens, more attention compute and less effective context. Next I build the BPE tokenizer myself, following Stanford CS336 Assignment 1.

hook: BPE is one rule applied over and over: find the most common pair, glue it together. That's the whole algorithm behind GPT's vocabulary.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GPT's vocabulary came from one rule repeated fifty thousand times. Find the most common pair. Glue it. Repeat.

0:15 QUESTION — Byte Pair Encoding started as a 1994 compression trick and became the standard after Sennrich et al. used it for translation in 2015. GPT-2, GPT-4, Llama 3 and most current LLMs use byte-level BPE. We run it by hand first so the code later has nothing hidden.

1:00 INTUITION — Start with the smallest pieces. Count every adjacent pair. The most frequent pair becomes a new symbol, and every occurrence gets replaced. Each merge shortens the sequence and grows the vocabulary by one. Stop when the vocabulary is the size you want. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Whiteboard on 'aaabdaaabac' (the Wikipedia example). Pairs: aa 4, ab 2, ba 1, bd 1, da 1, ac 1. Merge aa -> Z: 'ZabdZabac'. Now ab 2 is top: merge ab -> Y: 'ZYdZYac'. Merge ZY -> X: 'XdXac'. 11 symbols to 5, vocab grew by 3. Each merge: new length = old length - count(pair). Tie-breaking must be deterministic; CS336 picks the lexicographically greater pair.

5:30 CODE — def get_stats(ids: list[int]) -> dict[tuple[int,int], int]: count zip(ids, ids[1:]). def merge(ids, pair, idx) -> list[int]: walk with i, if ids[i:i+2] == pair append idx and i += 2 else append ids[i], i += 1. Training: ids = list(text.encode('utf-8')); for k in range(num_merges): stats = get_stats(ids); pair = max(stats, key=lambda p: (stats[p], p)); ids = merge(ids, pair, 256 + k); merges[pair] = 256 + k.

9:00 RECEIPT — Run on 'aaabdaaabac' using characters as the base. assert the three merges are ('a','a'), ('a','b'), ('Z','Y') in that order and the final string is 'XdXac'. Bytes version: after each merge, assert len(ids) == previous_len - stats[pair]. Overlap case: merge(list(b'aaa'), (97,97), 256) == [256, 97], not [256, 256].
10:30 MEASURE — Run 20 merges on one paragraph of this video's script; print each merge as bytes decoded, e.g. b'e ' then b'th' then b'the'. Plot sequence length vs merge number.
11:30 TAKEAWAY — BPE is greedy frequency-based compression; the merge list, in order, is the tokenizer. Interview line: the order of merges matters because later merges are built from earlier tokens.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Train a byte-level BPE tokenizer.
key_math: pair* = argmax_{(a,b)} count(a,b) (ties: lexicographically greater);  len_new = len_old - count(pair*);  |V| = 256 + num_merges
code_task: bpe_toy.py: get_stats(ids: list[int]) -> dict[tuple[int,int], int]; merge(ids, pair, idx) -> list[int]; train_toy(text: str, num_merges: int) -> dict[tuple[int,int], int] with new ids starting at 256.
receipt: assert merges on 'aaabdaaabac' are [('a','a'),('a','b'),('Z','Y')] and result == 'XdXac'; assert merge([97,97,97], (97,97), 256) == [256, 97]; each step len(ids_new) == len(ids_old) - stats[pair].
gotchas: Counting overlapping pairs in 'aaa' as two merges, the left-to-right merge only replaces one; non-deterministic tie-breaking from dict ordering so two runs disagree; merging across what should be word boundaries, which we fix with pre-tokenization in E05
interview_q: Walk me through how BPE builds a vocabulary. Answer: start from bytes, repeatedly count adjacent pairs across the corpus, merge the most frequent pair into a new token and record the merge, until the vocabulary reaches the target size; encoding replays merges in the same order.
explainer: We start with a tiny string, a a a b d a a a b a c. Eleven symbols.
Count every pair of neighbors. A A shows up four times. That is the winner.
Glue every A A into one new symbol. Call it Z. The whole string gets shorter.
Count the pairs again. Now A B is the most common pair, so it becomes Y.
And Z Y, which is really A A A B, becomes X. Eleven symbols are now five.
The list of merges, in the order we made them, is the tokenizer. Z, then Y, then X.
Real tokenizers start from the two hundred fifty six bytes and run this fifty thousand times.

Bracket pairs slide across the tiles; a tally table builds, with 'aa: 4' highlighted.
Pairs of 'a' tiles fuse into a 'Z' tile; the row contracts to 'ZabdZabac'.
New tally with 'ab: 2' highlighted; tiles fuse into Y, giving 'ZYdZYac'.
Z and Y fuse into X; final row 'XdXac'; counter shows 11 to 5.
A numbered list: 1. aa to Z, 2. ab to Y, 3. ZY to X, with a bracket labeled 'the tokenizer'.
The 16 by 16 byte grid, with a merge counter spinning up to 50,000.

hook: Naive BPE training recounts every pair after every merge. On TinyStories that's hours. Counting pre-tokens once turns it into seconds.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — My first BPE trainer took forever on TinyStories. One change, count each word once, made it fast. Here it is.

0:15 QUESTION — CS336 Assignment 1 asks you to train a byte-level BPE on TinyStories, 10,000 tokens, with a time budget. This is the same algorithm that produced GPT-2's 50,257-token vocabulary. Today: a 512-token version you can run on a laptop, written to the CS336 interface so it passes their tests.

1:00 INTUITION — Most of the text is the same words over and over. ' the' appears millions of times. So split the corpus into pre-tokens once, count how many times each distinct pre-token appears, and do BPE on that small table of unique byte sequences weighted by count. Merges never cross pre-token boundaries. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Corpus -> counter {pretoken_bytes_tuple: freq}. Pair count(a,b) = sum over pretokens w of freq(w) * occurrences of (a,b) in w. Pick argmax with ties broken by the lexicographically greater pair of bytes. Vocab: 256 byte tokens + special tokens + merges, so num_merges = vocab_size - 256 - len(special_tokens). Incremental update: when merging (a,b), only pretokens containing (a,b) change, so subtract their old pair counts and add their new ones instead of recounting everything.

5:30 CODE — def train_bpe(input_path: str, vocab_size: int, special_tokens: list[str]) -> tuple[dict[int, bytes], list[tuple[bytes, bytes]]]. Steps: read text; split on special tokens so nothing merges across '<|endoftext|>'; regex pre-tokenize with the GPT-2 pattern (explained fully in E05); counts = Counter(tuple(bytes([b]) for b in tok.encode('utf-8'))). vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)} plus specials. Loop: best = max(pair_counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (kv[1], kv[0]))[0]; merges.append(best); vocab[len(vocab)] = best[0] + best[1]; update affected pretokens and pair counts via an index pair -> set of pretokens.

9:00 RECEIPT — Clone stanford-cs336/assignment1-basics, wire adapters.run_train_bpe to your function, run pytest tests/test_train_bpe.py. It compares your vocab and merges to reference outputs and includes a speed test. All green. Then train on TinyStories validation with vocab_size=512, special_tokens=['<|endoftext|>']: assert len(vocab) == 512 and len(merges) == 512 - 256 - 1 = 255.
10:30 MEASURE — Wall-clock: naive recount vs incremental update on the same file, as a bar chart. Print the first 15 merges (b' t', b'he', b' a', b' the'...) and the longest learned token.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — BPE training is a counting problem; count unique pre-tokens once and update pair counts incrementally. Interview line: pre-tokenization is both a quality decision and the main speed trick in BPE training.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Encode and decode.
key_math: count(a,b) = sum_w freq(w) * #{(a,b) in w};  best = argmax (count, pair);  num_merges = vocab_size - 256 - |specials|
code_task: train_bpe(input_path: str, vocab_size: int, special_tokens: list[str]) -> (vocab: dict[int, bytes], merges: list[tuple[bytes, bytes]]), the CS336 A1 signature. Internals: pretoken Counter[tuple[bytes,...]], pair_counts dict[tuple[bytes,bytes], int], pair_to_words index for incremental updates.
receipt: pytest tests/test_train_bpe.py in stanford-cs336/assignment1-basics passes (reference merges/vocab match and speed test). On TinyStories valid with vocab_size=512: len(vocab) == 512, len(merges) == 255, b'<|endoftext|>' in vocab.values().
gotchas: Breaking ties by count only, so merges differ from the reference in order; letting merges span across <|endoftext|> because you pre-tokenized before splitting on special tokens; storing pretokens as bytes objects instead of tuples of bytes tokens, so merged tokens get split again
interview_q: How do you make BPE training fast on a multi-GB corpus? Answer: pre-tokenize and count unique pre-tokens once (in parallel over chunks split at special tokens), then run merges on the weighted unique set while updating pair counts incrementally for only the pre-tokens that contain the merged pair.
explainer: The corpus is millions of stories, but most of it is the same few thousand words repeated.
So first we cut the text into pre tokens and count each distinct one exactly once.
Now pair counts are weighted. A pair inside the word the counts once for every time the appears.
We take the most frequent pair, breaking ties by the larger pair, and record the merge.
Only words that contain that pair change. We update just those, instead of recounting everything.
Repeat until the vocabulary hits five hundred twelve. The early merges are spaces and common letter pairs.
Then we run the course's own test suite. Our merges match the reference merges, in the same order.

Text collapses into a table: ' the' 2.1M, ' a' 1.4M, ' was' 900k, each split into byte tiles.
The pair 'h','e' inside ' the' glows; its count adds 2.1M to a running pair tally.

hook: decode(encode(text)) always gives back your text. encode(decode(ids)) does not always give back your ids. Here's the counterexample.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — decode of encode always gives back your text. encode of decode does not always give back your ids. Here's why.

0:15 QUESTION — Training a tokenizer produces merges. Using it means applying those merges to new text, fast and exactly the way training did, and turning ids back into text without crashing on half a character. Every inference server, including vLLM's detokenizer, has to get this right while streaming.

1:00 INTUITION — Encoding replays history. Turn the text into bytes, then repeatedly find the adjacent pair whose merge was learned earliest and apply it, until no learned pair remains. Decoding is a lookup: each id maps to a bytes string, concatenate, then decode UTF-8. The catch is that a single token can end in the middle of a multi-byte character. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Merge rank r(a,b) = index in merges list. Encode = regex pre-tokenize (same pattern as training, E03), then per chunk: while some adjacent pair has finite rank: pick argmin rank, merge all its occurrences. Equivalence: this gives the same result as applying merges 0..n in order, because a pair created by merge k contains token k, so its rank is greater than k. Decode: bytes = concat(vocab[i]); text = bytes.decode('utf-8', errors='replace'). Round trip: decode(encode(s)) == s for every string s. Converse fails: ids [104, 105] ('h','i') decode to 'hi', which encodes to the single merged token if 'hi' was learned.

5:30 CODE — class Tokenizer: __init__(self, vocab: dict[int, bytes], merges: list[tuple[bytes, bytes]], special_tokens: list[str] | None = None). self.ranks = {pair: i for i, pair in enumerate(merges)}; self.inv = {b: i for i, b in vocab.items()}. def _encode_chunk(self, b: bytes) -> list[int]: parts = [bytes([x]) for x in b]; while len(parts) > 1: pair = min(zip(parts, parts[1:]), key=lambda p: self.ranks.get(p, inf)); if pair not in self.ranks: break; merge it. Return [self.inv[p] for p in parts]. def encode(self, text) -> list[int]: concatenate _encode_chunk(chunk.encode('utf-8')) over re.findall(PAT, text). def decode(self, ids: list[int]) -> str.

9:00 RECEIPT — Property test with hypothesis: @given(st.text()) def test_roundtrip(s): assert tok.decode(tok.encode(s)) == s, run with max_examples=2000 including emoji and Telugu. Consistency with training: for every pretoken w in the trainer's final counter, the merged byte tuple the trainer ended with equals [vocab[i] for i in tok._encode_chunk(w)]. Counterexample test: ids = [vocab_inv[b'h'], vocab_inv[b'i']]; assert tok.decode(ids) == 'hi' and tok.encode('hi') != ids when b'hi' is a learned token.
10:30 MEASURE — Encoding throughput in MB/s on 10 MB of TinyStories for the naive min-over-pairs loop; note the number, we speed it up in E08. Also compression ratio bytes/token for the 512 vocab.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Encoding replays merges by rank; decoding is concatenation; only text-to-ids-to-text is guaranteed to round-trip. Interview line: streaming detokenization must buffer bytes until they form complete UTF-8 characters, or users see replacement characters.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Pre-tokenization and special tokens.
key_math: rank(a,b) = position in merges;  encode: repeat merge argmin_rank pair;  decode(ids) = utf8(concat vocab[i]);  decode(encode(s)) = s for all s, encode(decode(ids)) != ids in general
code_task: tokenizer.py: class Tokenizer(vocab: dict[int, bytes], merges: list[tuple[bytes, bytes]], special_tokens=None) with _encode_chunk(b: bytes) -> list[int], encode(text: str) -> list[int] (regex chunks then _encode_chunk), decode(ids: list[int]) -> str (errors='replace'). Matches the CS336 A1 Tokenizer interface.
receipt: hypothesis: @given(st.text()) assert tok.decode(tok.encode(s)) == s (2000 examples); for each pretoken w the trainer saw, assert [vocab[i] for i in tok._encode_chunk(w)] == trainer_final_tuple[w]; assert tok.decode([id_h, id_i]) == 'hi' and tok.encode('hi') != [id_h, id_i].
gotchas: Decoding each token separately with .decode('utf-8') crashes on tokens that split a multi-byte character, concatenate bytes first; applying merges in a single left-to-right pass instead of by rank gives different tokens than training; quadratic re-scanning on long inputs if you do not chunk by pre-token
interview_q: Is tokenization invertible? Answer: decode(encode(text)) == text always holds for byte-level BPE, but encoding is not injective in reverse: many id sequences decode to the same text, and encode returns only the canonical one, which matters for things like constrained decoding and token healing.
explainer: Encoding starts from raw bytes. Space t h e s e is six separate byte tokens before any merging.
We look at every neighboring pair and ask, which of these was merged earliest in training?
Merge that pair everywhere, and look again. New pairs appear, each with its own rank from training.
When no neighboring pair was ever learned in training, we stop. What is left are the token ids.
Decoding goes the other way. Look up each id's bytes, glue them all together, then read as UTF-8.
Careful. One token can end halfway through a three byte character. Decode it alone and you get garbage.
Text to ids to text always round trips. Ids to text to ids does not, because the encoder picks one canonical answer.
explainer_visuals: The word ' these' as six tiles including the leading space, each labeled with its byte value.
Each adjacent pair gets a small rank badge from the merges list; the lowest, 'h e', glows.
'h' and 'e' fuse; new pair badges recalculate across the shorter row.
The row stops at two tiles ' the' and 'se'; their integer ids pop out below.
Ids map to byte strings that slide together into one byte row, which converts to text.
A Telugu character's three bytes split across two tokens; decoding just the first shows a replacement character.
Two loops: text to ids to text with a green check, ids to text to ids with a red cross and the 'h','i' example.
short: The h, i counterexample (MATH). Caption: 'Tokenizers are not invertible the way you think'

hook: GPT-2 runs a regex over your text before BPE ever sees it. Skip it and your tokenizer learns tokens like 'dog.' and 'dog!' separately.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Before BPE ever sees your text, GPT-2 runs one regex over it. Without it, 'dog.' and 'dog!' become different tokens.

0:15 QUESTION — OpenAI's tiktoken, Llama 3's tokenizer and CS336 all split text with a regex first and only merge inside the pieces. Plus there are special tokens like <|endoftext|> that must never be split or merged. Get either wrong and your ids will not match the real GPT-2, which means you cannot load its weights.

1:00 INTUITION — The regex cuts text into word-like chunks: contractions, a letter run with its leading space, a number run, a punctuation run, whitespace. BPE then runs inside each chunk independently, so merges can't glue a word to the punctuation after it. Special tokens get cut out before the regex and mapped straight to their reserved id. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Pattern (CS336 form of GPT-2): PAT = r"""'(?:[sdmt]|ll|ve|re)| ?\p{L}+| ?\p{N}+| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+""". Read it alternative by alternative: contractions 's 't 'd 'm 'll 've 're; optional space plus letters; optional space plus digits; optional space plus other symbols; whitespace not followed by non-whitespace, so the last space attaches to the next word; any remaining whitespace. Needs the third-party regex module for \p{L}. GPT-4's cl100k changes the digit rule to \p{N}{1,3} and makes contractions case-insensitive.

5:30 CODE — import regex as re. PAT = the GPT-2 pattern. def pretokenize(text) -> list[str]: re.findall(PAT, text). Special tokens: sort by length descending, pattern = '(' + '|'.join(map(re.escape, specials)) + ')', re.split keeps the delimiters; for each part, if it is a special emit its id, else encode each pretoken chunk with _encode_chunk. Load GPT-2's vocab.json and merges.txt and undo GPT-2's bytes_to_unicode mapping to get real bytes. Add encode_iterable(iterable) -> Iterator[int] for streaming files.

9:00 RECEIPT — enc = tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2'). For 1,000 TinyStories samples and a stress set (emoji, Telugu, code, '  multiple   spaces', "I'll"): assert my_tok.encode(s) == enc.encode(s, allowed_special={'<|endoftext|>'}). Specials: assert my_tok.encode('a<|endoftext|>b') == [64, 50256, 65]. Overlapping specials: with ['<|endoftext|>', '<|endoftext|><|endoftext|>'] the double one is kept as one token. Then pytest tests/test_tokenizer.py in CS336 A1.

10:30 MEASURE — Show re.findall output on a sentence, chunk by chunk. Retrain my 512 BPE with and without pre-tokenization and list tokens that only appear without it, such as 'dog.' style word-plus-punctuation merges and cross-word merges.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Pre-tokenization decides which merges are allowed; special tokens bypass BPE entirely. Interview line: a token-id mismatch of even one id against the reference tokenizer silently breaks pretrained weights, so test against tiktoken.
12:00 NEXT — Next: tiktoken vs SentencePiece vs HF tokenizers.
key_math: text -> split on specials -> regex chunks c_1..c_k -> BPE(c_i) independently;  ids = concat_i BPE(c_i);  special s -> fixed id (GPT-2: <|endoftext|> = 50256)
code_task: Extend Tokenizer: PAT (GPT-2 regex, regex module), pretokenize(text) -> list[str], special-token splitting with longest-first alternation, from_files(vocab_path, merges_path, special_tokens) handling GPT-2's bytes_to_unicode, encode_iterable(iterable) -> Iterator[int].
receipt: For 1,000 TinyStories samples plus a stress set: assert my_tok.encode(s) == tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2').encode(s, allowed_special={'<|endoftext|>'}); assert my_tok.encode('a<|endoftext|>b') == [64, 50256, 65]; CS336 tests/test_tokenizer.py passes.
gotchas: Using the standard re module, which does not support \p{L}; tiktoken's encode raises on text containing <|endoftext|> unless you pass allowed_special (or use encode_ordinary); GPT-2's vocab.json stores bytes through the bytes_to_unicode remapping, so ' the' appears as 'Ġthe' and must be mapped back
interview_q: Why do GPT-style tokenizers pre-tokenize with a regex before BPE? Answer: it prevents merges across category boundaries like word and punctuation or across words, which gives cleaner, more reusable tokens, and it makes training and encoding parallel per chunk; special tokens are split out first so they map to reserved ids and are never merged.
explainer: Without any rules, BPE happily merges a word with the punctuation after it. Dog period and dog exclamation become separate tokens.
So GPT-2 first runs a regular expression that cuts text into chunks. Merges can only happen inside a chunk.
Letters stay with the space in front of them. Space dog is one chunk. The period is its own chunk.
Contractions get their own rule, so apostrophe L L is a chunk and I is a chunk.
Runs of spaces leave their last space for the next word, which keeps space plus word tokens consistent.
Special tokens are cut out before any of this. End of text goes straight to id fifty thousand two hundred fifty six.
Then we compare against OpenAI's tiktoken on a thousand real stories. Every single id matches.
explainer_visuals: Tokens 'dog.' , 'dog!' , 'dog?' appear as three separate vocab entries with a red wasted badge.
A sentence gets vertical cut lines; each chunk gets its own box.
The sentence 'I saw a dog.' splitting into 'I', ' saw', ' a', ' dog', '.'.
"I'll" splitting into 'I' and "'ll" with the contraction alternative of the regex highlighted.
Three spaces before 'cat'; two become a whitespace chunk, the third joins ' cat'.
The string '<|endoftext|>' lifted out whole and stamped with 50256, bypassing the BPE machinery.
Two id streams side by side scrolling, with a counter '1000 / 1000 match' and a green check.

x_post: GPT-2 splits text with a regex before BPE, so merges never cross word/punctuation boundaries, and <|endoftext|> bypasses BPE entirely (id 50256). My tokenizer now matches tiktoken's gpt2 encoding id-for-id. Code + video: [link]

This is what makes loading pretrained GPT-2 weights possible later.

hook: The same paragraph costs a different number of tokens in GPT-2, GPT-4o, Qwen and T5. Here's the table, and why Telugu pays the most.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same paragraph, four tokenizers, very different token counts. For some languages the bill is several times higher.

0:15 QUESTION — OpenAI uses tiktoken BPE. Llama 2 and T5 used SentencePiece. Most open models ship through Hugging Face tokenizers. Picking a vocabulary size is a real design decision: bigger vocab means shorter sequences but a bigger embedding table and rarer tokens. Llama 3 went from 32k to 128k for exactly this trade.

1:00 INTUITION — BPE builds up: start from bytes, merge frequent pairs. Unigram LM, from SentencePiece, carves down: start from a huge candidate vocabulary and prune the pieces whose removal hurts likelihood least. SentencePiece also treats the space as a visible symbol, the lower one-eighth block, so it needs no language-specific pre-tokenizer. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Unigram LM: P(x) = prod_i p(x_i) over a segmentation x of the text; pick the segmentation with max probability by Viterbi; train with EM, then prune the bottom 20 percent or so of pieces each round. Tradeoff: sequence length T roughly falls like 1/log V in practice, while embedding params grow as V d. Tokens per character and bytes per token are the two metrics we tabulate. Fertility for a language = tokens per word.

5:00 CODE — Texts: English paragraph, Python function, Telugu paragraph, Hindi paragraph, numbers like 1234567. Tokenizers: tiktoken gpt2 (50,257), cl100k_base (~100k), o200k_base (~200k); HF AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B') (byte-level BPE, about 151k) and 'google-t5/t5-small' (SentencePiece unigram, 32k); plus my own 512 BPE. Also train SentencePiece myself: sentencepiece.SentencePieceTrainer.train(input=..., model_prefix=..., vocab_size=8000, model_type='unigram') and again with model_type='bpe'.

9:00 RECEIPT — For every byte-level tokenizer assert decode(encode(s)) == s on all texts. For T5, show that it does not round-trip exactly (unknown characters and whitespace normalization), and print the diff. Report each tokenizer's vocab size from the object itself, e.g. enc.n_vocab and len(hf_tok), and confirm them against the published numbers.
10:30 MEASURE — Table: rows = texts, columns = tokenizers, cells = tokens and bytes/token. Bar chart of Telugu tokens relative to English for each tokenizer. Show how o200k narrows the gap.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Byte-level BPE never fails to encode; unigram SentencePiece gives probabilistic segmentations; vocabulary size trades sequence length against embedding size. Interview line: a bigger vocab shortens sequences, which cuts attention cost and extends effective context, at the cost of a larger embedding and softmax.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Why LLMs can't spell.
key_math: Unigram: x* = argmax_x prod_i p(x_i) (Viterbi), trained by EM + pruning;  cost tradeoff: embedding/head params = V d, attention ~ T^2;  metric: bytes/token, tokens/word
code_task: tok_compare.py: tokenizers dict name -> (encode, decode, vocab_size) for tiktoken gpt2/cl100k_base/o200k_base, HF Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B and google-t5/t5-small, my BPE-512, and SentencePiece unigram/bpe models trained at vocab 8000; table(texts) -> pandas DataFrame of token counts and bytes/token.
receipt: For all byte-level tokenizers: assert dec(enc(s)) == s for every text; vocab sizes read from the objects (enc.n_vocab == 50257 for gpt2); T5 round-trip failure shown with a printed diff rather than asserted equal.
gotchas: Comparing HF tokenizers with add_special_tokens=True, which adds BOS/EOS and inflates counts; assuming Llama 2's SentencePiece model is unigram, it is SentencePiece BPE with byte fallback; T5's tokenizer normalizes and maps unknown characters to <unk>, so lossless round trips are not guaranteed
interview_q: How would you choose the vocabulary size for a new multilingual LLM? Answer: measure bytes per token and fertility per language on your data mix across candidate sizes; larger vocabularies shorten sequences and help underrepresented scripts but grow the embedding and output layer and make rare tokens undertrained, so modern models land around 128k to 256k.
explainer: Two families of tokenizers. BPE builds its vocabulary up by merging. Unigram carves it down by pruning.
Unigram scores every possible way to cut a word and keeps the most probable one.
SentencePiece also treats the space as a real symbol, so it needs no rules about words.
Now the experiment. The same paragraph goes through GPT-2, GPT-4's cl100k, GPT-4o's o200k, Qwen and T5.
For English the counts are close. The bigger vocabularies win, but only by a little, maybe ten or twenty percent.
For Telugu the spread is huge. Older tokenizers fall back to bytes and the count balloons.
Bigger vocabulary means shorter sequences and cheaper attention. But you pay for it with a bigger embedding table.
explainer_visuals: Split screen: left, small tiles merging into bigger ones; right, a big pile of pieces being trimmed away.
The word 'tokenization' with several segmentation paths drawn as a lattice; the best path highlighted.
A sentence with each space replaced by a small visible block character.
Five tokenizer logos as plain labeled boxes, each receiving the same paragraph.
A grouped bar chart for English with five similar bars.
The Telugu group with GPT-2's bar towering over o200k's.
A seesaw with 'sequence length' on one side and 'embedding params V times d' on the other.
short: Telugu vs English bars across tokenizers (MEASURE). Caption: 'Your language decides your AI bill'
yt_title: tiktoken vs SentencePiece vs Hugging Face Tokenizers, measured
x_post: Same Telugu paragraph: GPT-2's tokenizer falls back to bytes and balloons; o200k cuts it way down. BPE builds vocab up, unigram prunes it down. Measured tokens/byte for 6 tokenizers on 5 kinds of text. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Compared six tokenizers (tiktoken gpt2/cl100k/o200k, Qwen2.5, T5 unigram, and my own BPE) on English, code, Telugu, Hindi and numbers. English is roughly a wash; Telugu costs several times more tokens on older vocabularies. I also trained SentencePiece unigram vs BPE on the same data to see the algorithmic difference directly.

hook: The model can't count the r's in strawberry because it never saw the letters. Here are the actual tokens behind the famous failures.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Ask a model how many r's are in strawberry and it might say two. It never saw the letters. Let me show you what it saw.

0:15 QUESTION — Letter counting, reversing words, multi-digit arithmetic, and glitch tokens like SolidGoldMagikarp are all famous LLM failures. Karpathy's tokenizer lecture argues a lot of them trace back to tokenization. We check that claim with real tokenizers instead of repeating it.

1:00 INTUITION — The model receives one integer for a chunk like 'berry'. The letters inside are not in its input at all; it has to have memorized the spelling of each token from context. Numbers are cut in arbitrary places, so 1234 and 1235 might look nothing alike. A glitch token is an id that exists in the vocabulary but barely appeared in training, so its embedding is untrained. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — For spelling: input is ids, P(answer | ids); character identity inside a token is only available through the learned embedding E[id], a 768-dim vector in GPT-2. For glitch tokens: an embedding row that receives almost no gradient stays near its init, so its norm and its nearest neighbors look odd. Check: ||E[id]|| compared against the vocabulary's typical norm, and cosine similarity to the centroid.

5:00 CODE — For each tokenizer (gpt2, cl100k_base, o200k_base): print tokens for ' strawberry', 'strawberry', ' Strawberry'; numbers '1234 + 5678', '12345678'; ' SolidGoldMagikarp'; 'trailing space ' vs 'trailing space'. Use [enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t) for t in enc.encode(s)] to show the byte chunks. Load GPT-2 from transformers, take E = model.transformer.wte.weight, compute norms, and list the ids whose embeddings are closest to the mean embedding.

9:00 RECEIPT — assert len(tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2').encode(' SolidGoldMagikarp')) == 1 while it is several tokens in o200k_base. Number chunking: in cl100k_base, digits are grouped at most 3 at a time, so assert all(len(enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t)) <= 3 for t in enc.encode('12345678')). Show GPT-2 groups digits inconsistently by comparing two nearby numbers.
10:30 MEASURE — Table of token splits for the strawberry variants across three tokenizers. Histogram of GPT-2 embedding norms with the SolidGoldMagikarp-family ids marked at the low or odd end.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Many classic LLM failures are input-representation problems, not reasoning problems. Interview line: models are bad at character-level tasks because characters aren't in their input; digit-splitting rules like cl100k's 1-to-3 digit groups were added partly to help arithmetic.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Tokenizing a dataset fast.
key_math: model sees ids, not chars: P(y | id_1..id_T);  characters inside a token available only via E[id];  glitch token: ||E[id]|| approx init norm (barely trained)
code_task: tok_failures.py: show(enc, s) -> list of byte chunks via enc.decode_single_token_bytes; cases for spelling, numbers, glitch tokens, trailing whitespace across gpt2/cl100k_base/o200k_base; embed_norms(wte (50257, 768)) -> histogram and outlier ids.
receipt: assert len(tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2').encode(' SolidGoldMagikarp')) == 1 and len(tiktoken.get_encoding('o200k_base').encode(' SolidGoldMagikarp')) > 1; in cl100k_base every token of '12345678' decodes to at most 3 bytes.
gotchas: Forgetting the leading space, ' strawberry' and 'strawberry' tokenize differently and give different stories; claiming a specific split from memory without printing it, the splits differ by tokenizer and version; reading decode() of one token that is a partial UTF-8 sequence and seeing replacement characters
interview_q: Why do LLMs struggle to count letters in a word? Answer: the input is token ids, so a word like strawberry arrives as a few multi-character chunks and the model only knows their spelling indirectly through learned embeddings; character-level tasks require recovering information that tokenization hid.
explainer: We type strawberry. The model never receives those ten letters. It receives a couple of integers.
To count the r's, the model has to remember how each chunk is spelled. Nothing in the input says so.
Numbers get the same treatment. In GPT-2, two nearby numbers can be chopped in completely different places.
GPT-4's tokenizer forces digits into groups of at most three. Arithmetic gets a consistent alphabet.
Then there are glitch tokens. Space SolidGoldMagikarp is one single token in GPT-2's fifty thousand entry vocabulary.
It came from scraped usernames and barely appeared in the model's training text. Its embedding was barely trained.
Plot every embedding's length. The glitch tokens sit in a strange corner, close to where they started.
explainer_visuals: The word 'strawberry' collapses into two or three colored token chips with ids beneath.
One chip opens like a box showing letters inside, labeled 'not visible to the model'.
'1234' and '1235' each splitting differently, shown with mismatched chip boundaries.
A long number split into neat three-digit chips with a regex snippet beside it.
The string ' SolidGoldMagikarp' mapping to one chip in the GPT-2 vocab table.
A tokenizer corpus pile containing the name, versus a model training corpus pile where it is almost absent.
A histogram of embedding norms with a few marked outliers labeled glitch tokens.

A lot of 'reasoning failures' are input-representation failures.

hook: Tokenizing 2 GB of text on one core can take an hour. Split at <|endoftext|>, use every core, write uint16, and it's minutes.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — My tokenizer is correct. On 2 gigabytes of TinyStories it's also painfully slow. Let's make it use every core.

0:15 QUESTION — Pretraining reads billions of tokens, and nobody tokenizes on the fly. You tokenize once into a flat binary file and memory-map it, which is how nanoGPT and CS336 both feed their training loops. This file is what M06's data loader will read.

1:00 INTUITION — Tokenization is embarrassingly parallel as long as you never cut through a document. So find chunk boundaries at <|endoftext|>, give each chunk to a worker process, and concatenate the results. Store ids as 2-byte unsigned ints, since a 10k vocab fits in 65,536. Then np.memmap lets the trainer read random windows without loading the file. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Bytes on disk = num_tokens * 2 for uint16 vs 8 for int64, a 4x saving. Throughput = input MB / seconds. Expected speedup with P processes is at most P, minus overhead for pickling results back to the parent. Compression ratio of your tokenizer sets file size: tokens = bytes / ratio. Assert max_id < 2^16 = 65,536 before casting, or ids wrap silently.

5:30 CODE — def find_chunk_boundaries(f, num_chunks: int, split_token: bytes) -> list[int]: seek to evenly spaced byte offsets, read forward in 4 KB windows until you find b'<|endoftext|>', return sorted unique offsets (the CS336 helper). def encode_chunk(args) -> np.ndarray: read bytes [start, end), decode, tok.encode, return np.array(ids, dtype=np.uint16). with multiprocessing.Pool(os.cpu_count()) as pool: parts = pool.map(encode_chunk, ranges). Write with np.concatenate(parts).tofile('train.bin'). Speed the inner encode: cache _encode_chunk results per pretoken with functools.lru_cache, since words repeat.

9:00 RECEIPT — Correctness: ids = np.memmap('valid.bin', dtype=np.uint16, mode='r'); assert tok.decode(ids.tolist()) == open('valid.txt').read() on the validation split (or on 100 random documents for train). assert ids.max() < len(vocab). Parallel equals serial: assert np.array_equal(parallel_ids, serial_ids) on a 50 MB slice. Reference: tiktoken's encode_ordinary_batch throughput on the same text as a published-implementation comparison.

10:30 MEASURE — MB/s for: naive single process, plus pretoken cache, plus multiprocessing at 1, 2, 4, 8 cores. Plot speedup vs cores with the ideal line. Final .bin size and token count for TinyStories train and valid. This MB/s number goes on the resume line.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Tokenize once, in parallel, split at document boundaries, into a uint16 memmap. Interview line: you chunk at special tokens so no worker splits a document and the parallel output is byte-identical to the serial one.
12:00 NEXT — Next: A GPT forward pass in one picture.
key_math: disk bytes = N_tokens * 2 (uint16);  speedup_P <= P;  N_tokens = N_bytes / compression_ratio;  require max_id < 65536
code_task: tokenize_dataset.py: find_chunk_boundaries(f, num_chunks, b'<|endoftext|>') -> list[int]; encode_chunk((path, start, end)) -> np.ndarray[uint16]; main(input_path, out_path, n_proc) writes a flat uint16 .bin; lru_cache on per-pretoken encoding. Output read via np.memmap(path, dtype=np.uint16, mode='r').
receipt: assert np.array_equal(parallel_ids, serial_ids) on a 50 MB slice; assert tok.decode(np.memmap('valid.bin', dtype=np.uint16, mode='r').tolist()) == valid_text; assert ids.max() < vocab_size; throughput compared against tiktoken encode_ordinary_batch on the same file.
gotchas: Chunk boundaries that land mid-character or mid-document give different ids than the serial run; casting to uint16 with a vocab over 65,535 wraps ids silently; returning Python lists from workers makes pickling the bottleneck, return numpy arrays
interview_q: How would you tokenize a 1 TB pretraining corpus? Answer: shard at document boundaries, run the tokenizer in parallel across processes and machines, cache encodings of repeated pre-tokens, write fixed-width integer shards (uint16 if the vocab fits, else uint32), and verify by decoding samples back to the source text.
explainer: Two gigabytes of stories, one CPU core, one tokenizer. This is going to take a while.
But stories are independent. We can split the file and hand pieces to different cores.
The cut points matter. We slide each one forward to the next end of text token.
Each worker tokenizes its piece. The words repeat constantly, so we cache each word's tokens.
The results get glued in order and written as two byte integers. Four times smaller than int64.
Training will memory map this file and read random windows without ever loading it all.
Speedup against core count. Close to the ideal line at first, then process overhead bends it.
explainer_visuals: A long progress bar crawling, a single CPU core icon glowing.
The file as a long bar split into eight segments, each sliding to its own core icon.
Evenly spaced cut markers each nudge right until they snap onto an '<|endoftext|>' marker.
Eight workers processing in parallel; a cache box catching ' the' and returning its id instantly.
Arrays concatenating into one long strip; a size label shrinks from 8 bytes per token to 2.
A file icon with a window frame sliding over it, pulling out a short strip of ids.
A line chart of speedup vs cores with a dashed ideal line and the measured line bending below it.
